criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water and sanitation service access in Usoma, a rural lakeshore community near Kisumu, Kenya, including lack of piped/safe water, reliance on lake water and distant taps/vendors, open defecation, and inadequate pit latrines.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper passes because it empirically examines community governance institutions (village elders/chiefs, barazas, leadership trust, community-based groups such as UWASH) and perceived local government neglect and unequal resource distribution constraining water and sanitation collective action. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, it fails (c2 = no): the empirical investigation focuses on knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP), community mobilization/social capital, and broad socioeconomic/macro-governance background (unemployment, low income, power asymmetries with construction firms, and general feelings of municipal neglect). It does not empirically analyse any specific legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, formal tariff/cost-recovery rules, administrative burden, enforcement rules, or utility regulatory structure; the brief mention of LVSWSB and KIWASCO's pro-poor model in the Discussion is secondary background cited to Maoulidi, 2010).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical data collected via participatory photovoice with 8 women (June-August 2013), comprising participant photography, 32 individual photo-elicitation interviews (60-90 minutes per photo), and a follow-up group discussion analysed thematically in NVivo 10.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative evidence on community and household water and sanitation access, safe water availability, vendor water affordability (20 Kenyan shillings per 20-litre jerry can), open defecation, and toilet construction barriers.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (women in Usoma, Western Kenya; individual/community level), study exposures (ecological conditions, KAP, community collective action, and broad structural factors like unemployment and perceived marginalisation), outcomes (water/sanitation practices and access challenges), and study design (participatory photovoice qualitative study) are all clearly identifiable, though the exposure is outside the review's rule-type legal/administrative scope.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (interviews conducted in DhoLuo and translated into English by the research team).

evidence_quotes.quote: Though located by the second largest freshwater lake in the world, the community had no access to safe water at the time of this study. The nearest safe water source was a tap located about 3 kms away on the premises of a Coca-Cola bottling plant.
If the administration was fair to provide us with water most of our problems will be solved. Sometime we need to talk about the way we have been cheated and neglected over the years (Betty).

We have a water and sanitation committee that is trying to mobilise people to solve these problems, but the problem is how to raise capital to either build public toilets or help people construct their own toilets.
The study was undertaken between June and August, 2013. Eight women participated in the study over the entire period.
Considering the level of unemployment and incomes in the community, it is very unlikely households can afford to buy the required quantities from vendors.

raw_response.exposure: Ecological setting (proximity to Lake Victoria, sand harvesting, industrial pollution), community collective action (women's groups, barazas, village elders/leadership trust), and broad structural factors (unemployment, low incomes, power relations, and perceived local government neglect/marginalisation)
raw_response.outcome: Household and community water and sanitation practices and access challenges (reliance on unsafe lake water, vendor water affordability constraints, open defecation, pit latrine conditions, and barriers to communal toilet/borehole construction)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Women in Usoma, a rural lakeshore community (~3,000 residents) 15 km from Kisumu in Western Kenya; snowball sample of 8 women (ages 22-54) completing 32 photo-elicitation interviews and 1 group discussion (unit of analysis: individual and community)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. While this qualitative photovoice study examines household/community water and sanitation access and affordability in rural Kenya (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes), its empirical focus is on knowledge, attitudes, practices, community collective action/mobilisation, unemployment/poverty, and general perceptions of municipal neglect rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access. (Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines community governance institutions and perceived institutional/government marginalisation.)
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative participatory action research using photovoice (individual photo-elicitation interviews and group discussion)
